title: India's Vision of a New World Order

cards.h: A rising power writes its own script
cards.b:
India's leaders say the world order built in 1945 no longer reflects today's power. They want a multipolar world, a reformed UN and a bigger role for the Global South. They also say India should be a 'Vishwa Bandhu' (friend of the world) and a 'leading power', not a mere balancer.

This lesson covers what India says it wants, the tools it uses (G20 2023, the Voice of the Global South summits, BRICS 2026, solar and disaster alliances, digital public goods) and the criticism that rhetoric runs ahead of capacity.

It is also a good place to apply IR theory: Zakaria's 'rise of the rest', Acharya's 'multiplex world', and the idea of a 'swing state'.

cards.h: From Nehru's 'one world' to Modi's 'Vishwa Bandhu'
cards.b:
The ambition is not new. Nehru spoke of 'one world' and tried to shape global norms on disarmament and decolonisation. Indira Gandhi led the demand for a New International Economic Order. After 1991 the stress shifted to economic strength and strategic partnerships.

What is new is the language: 'leading power', 'Vishwa Bandhu' and 'Viksit Bharat'. And what is new in method: India now offers solutions (solar, digital, vaccines) and joins many groupings at once, instead of speaking only for the poor in the abstract.

cards.h: The building blocks of India's vision
cards.b:
• Multipolarity: a world with several centres, in Asia as well as globally. A multipolar Asia matters because India does not want China to dominate it.
  • Strategic autonomy / multi-alignment: India takes decisions on its interests, with no formal allies. S. Jaishankar's The India Way (2020) lays it out.
  • Reformed multilateralism: UNSC, IMF quotas, WTO dispute settlement and the global financial architecture must change.
  • Rules, not might: respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity and international law, and 'dialogue and diplomacy' over war. Modi told Putin at Samarkand in 2022 that today's era is not an era of war.
  • Civilisational values: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (the world is one family), the G20 theme of 2023: 'One Earth, One Family, One Future'.

cards.h: Three ways to read the new order
cards.b:
Fareed Zakaria, The Post-American World (2008)

The 'rise of the rest': China, India and others grow while US dominance relatively declines. Not a decline of America, but the rise of others.

Amitav Acharya, The End of the American World Order (2014)

The old Western-led order is ending. What follows is a multiplex world, like a cinema with many screens: no single power and many actors, including regional bodies and non-state groups.

Kishore Mahbubani, The New Asian Hemisphere (2008)

Power is shifting from West to Asia. The West must share power in global institutions.

India's own voice stresses that it is a swing state (a term from Kliman and Fontaine, 2012): a democracy that cannot be taken for granted by any camp.

cards.h: G20 2023 and the Voice of the Global South
cards.b:
• Voice of Global South Summit: first held virtually on 12–13 January 2023 with over 100 countries. Further editions followed in November 2023 and August 2024.
  • G20 presidency (December 2022–November 2023): the New Delhi Leaders' Declaration was adopted by consensus on 9 September 2023, despite splits over Ukraine. The African Union was admitted as a permanent member.
  • Global South priorities: debt relief, climate finance, digital public infrastructure, reform of multilateral development banks, food and energy security.

India offers itself as a bridge: able to speak with the US and Russia, the West and the South.

In 2026 India chaired BRICS (summit in New Delhi, 12–13 September 2026, with a consensus declaration despite sharp Iran–UAE differences) and hosted the AI Impact Summit (February 2026), which ended with a New Delhi Declaration backed by around 88 countries and organisations.

• International Solar Alliance (ISA): launched with France at COP21, Paris, in November 2015. Headquarters at Gurugram.
  • Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI): launched in 2019.
  • Global Biofuels Alliance: launched at the 2023 G20.
  • Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment), launched in 2022.
  • Digital public infrastructure: UPI, Aadhaar-style identity and the 'India Stack' offered to other states.
  • Vaccine Maitri (2021) and development aid through ITEC (1964).

At COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) Modi announced a net-zero target for 2070 and the 'Panchamrit' goals. India stresses climate justice and common but differentiated responsibilities.

• UN Security Council: India wants permanent membership and has said veto power should not stay with the current five if the Council expands. It supports text-based negotiations (IGN) and works with the G4. See the later lesson.
  • Bretton Woods: more votes for developing countries at the IMF and World Bank (the 16th review of quotas).
  • WTO: a permanent solution for public stockholding for food security, and restoring the Appellate Body.
  • Terrorism: India has pushed since 1996 for a Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism.
  • New domains: rules for AI, cyberspace and space.

India argues that a legitimate order needs a legitimate voice for 1.4 billion people.

Supporters point to the G20 consensus and the African Union seat. Critics say India's 'Global South' leadership is thin on money (aid is a fraction of China's), that it avoided firm stands on Ukraine and Gaza, and that the Global South is too diverse to speak with one voice.

China is a rival claimant to the Global South mantle. In BRICS and SCO the two sit together but compete for leadership.

There is also the question whether India wants to change the order or to join it at the top table. Many scholars say India is a revisionist within the system: it wants more power in the rules, not new rules.

The year 2025–26 tested every pillar. US tariffs, the Iran war and the Sindoor crisis showed the limits of autonomy. India answered by diversifying trade (UK, EFTA, EU deals), pressing BRICS to keep a balanced line and hosting summits in New Delhi in 2026.

Viksit Bharat 2047, the goal of a developed India by its 100th year of independence, ties the foreign policy vision to economic growth. Without growth, the voice will not carry.

A good conclusion line: India's new-order claim rests on three legs: economic weight, public goods and balanced diplomacy. Each leg needs further strength.

Structure: (1) context: shifting power; (2) India's principles: autonomy, multipolarity, reform; (3) tools: G20, VOGSS, BRICS, ISA, DPI; (4) reforms asked: UNSC, IMF, WTO; (5) critique: capacity gap, selective voice; (6) way forward.

Quote one thinker (Zakaria or Acharya) and one 2023–26 event to earn marks.

quiz.q: Who wrote 'The End of the American World Order' (2014)?
quiz.w: Amitav Acharya, who describes a 'multiplex world'.

quiz.q: Zakaria's 'rise of the rest' appears in:
o: The Tragedy of Great Power Politics

quiz.q: India's G20 presidency culminated in a summit in New Delhi on:
Which body became a permanent G20 member at the New Delhi summit?
quiz.w: The African Union joined as a permanent member.

quiz.q: The International Solar Alliance was launched in:
quiz.w: At COP21, Paris, November 2015, by India and France.

quiz.q: India's net-zero target announced at COP26 is for the year:
The term 'swing state' in this context comes from:
quiz.w: Daniel Kliman and Richard Fontaine, Global Swing States (2012).

quiz.q: India has pushed since 1996 for adoption of the:
o: Treaty on Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons
quiz.w: The CCIT, proposed by India in 1996, remains stuck at the UN.

quiz.q: The BRICS summit of September 2026 was held in:
quiz.w: At Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, 12-13 September 2026.
